For ten students whose Unit 3 explanations did not meet the study's completeness criteria, I compared the original responses with later closed-resource reconstructions of the same photosynthesis mechanism. The record used to assess an explanation can change which scientific relationships are visible. In a study included in the scoping review, Luis's shorter English translation made an ecological distinction less explicit than his bilingual account. In my classroom inquiry, S20's closed-resource reconstruction omitted photosynthetic relationships expressed in an earlier response. The cases arose under different task and language conditions. Read together, they caution against treating an absent relationship in one response as a complete account of a student's understanding.

My projects examined the grounds for inferring scientific understanding from students' work. A teacher may judge an explanation incomplete on scientific grounds and still encounter a student who questions that interpretation. What remains less visible in an assessment record is how such a judgment is explained and whether the student can influence what happens next.

+

My projects examined the grounds for inferring scientific understanding from students' work. They did not establish how students could influence the judgments teachers made from that work. A teacher might identify an incomplete causal pathway and choose what students should revisit, yet the student could have reasons for questioning that interpretation. Studying the interaction would require attention to what each participant considered adequate evidence and to how their judgments shaped the next classroom activity.

-

The judgment made about a student's response can shape what the class investigates next. Teacher noticing offers a way to examine how reasoning becomes available for consideration; epistemic agency and rightful presence raise further questions about who can influence the direction and standards of inquiry. The linguistic and representational forms of students' contributions shape both the evidence available and the judgments made from it.

+

The questions emerging from my projects extend from the interpretation of a response to the decisions made after it. Research on teacher noticing examines how student reasoning becomes available for consideration. Work on epistemic agency and rightful presence asks who can influence the questions and standards guiding a classroom inquiry. I read these perspectives alongside scholarship on language and scientific modelling, where the evidence students can offer is shaped by the opportunities they have to participate.
